Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Tom Cruise expounds on his beliefs in Scientology in a 2004 video that made its way onto the Internet this week. Tom Cruise appears with his wife, Katie Holmes, at a movie premiere earlier this month. "I think it's a privilege to call yourself a Scientologist, and it's something you have to earn," Cruise says at the beginning of the video. Cruise says he's "driven ... by the opportunity to really help, for the first time, change people's lives. I'm absolutely, uncompromisingly dedicated to that." The video was shown at a 2004 Scientology ceremony honoring Cruise for his humanitarian work. Church of Scientology officials said it can be viewed at any of its churches, but it created a stir this week when what the church calls a pirated and edited version appeared on YouTube. The video has since been taken off YouTube, but an interview portion remained available on the celebrity Web site gawker.com on Thursday.  Watch snippets of Cruise video » . "The Cruise Indoctrination Video Scientology Tried To Suppress" is the title of gawker.com's presentation. "You have to watch this video," the site says. "It shows Tom Cruise, with all the wide-eyed fervor that he brings to the promotion of a movie, making the argument for Scientology," which it calls "the bizarre 20th-century religion.  Watch "Showbiz Tonight" discussion of Cruise video » . Cruise talks over a repetitive guitar-riff soundtrack, and appears to be answering questions, though an interviewer is not seen or heard. A second part of the video, made available to CNN by the publisher of a new unauthorized biography of Cruise, shows Cruise accepting Scientology's Freedom Medal of Valor award and exchanging military-like salutes with Scientology chairman David Miscavige to audience applause. The publisher denies leaking other parts of the video to the Web. In the video by the publisher, Cruise also salutes a portrait of L. Ron Hubbard, cited on the church's Web site as the founder of "the only major religion founded in the 20th century." Hubbard's biography cites his accomplishments as everything from mariner and horticulturalist to author and humanitarian. In the video, Cruise puts emphasis on the latter role. A Scientologist "has the ability to create new realities and improve conditions," Cruise says. On its Web site, the Church of Scientology highlights its humanitarian work, from anti-drug campaigns in places from Minnesota to Taiwan to teacher training in India. The Web site defines Scientology as "the study of truth." Cruise embraces that in the video. "If you're a Scientologist, ... you see things the way they are," Cruise says. He also says he finds peace in the religion. "The more you know as a Scientologist, you don't become overwhelmed by it," according to Cruise. The unauthorized biography of Cruise is by author Andrew Morton. A Cruise spokesperson and the Church of Scientology have disputed the book, saying Morton did not seek their comment. "Accuracy and truth were not on Morton's agenda," according to a church statement. Morton denies that and says Cruise, who he calls "a towering figure on the international scene," and his faith are worthy of scrutiny. "Tom Cruise has done remarkable work for his faith over the past few years," Morton said. "If it wasn't for him the Church of Scientology would be a shadow of what it is today." E-mail to a friend . CNN's Brad Lendon, David Mattingly and Don Lemon contributed to this report.

A second portion of the video, provided to CNN by the publisher of a new unauthorized biography of Cruise, shows him accepting Scientology’s Freedom Medal of Valor award and exchanging military-style salutes with Scientology Chairman David Miscavige as the audience applauds. The publisher denies leaking other portions of the video to the Web.

In the video provided by the publisher, Cruise also salutes a portrait of L. Ron Hubbard, identified on the church’s website as the founder of “the only major religion founded in the 20th century.”

A Scientologist “has the ability to create new realities and improve conditions,” Cruise says.

“Accuracy and truth were not on Morton’s agenda,” the church said in a statement.

Morton denies that claim and says Cruise—whom he calls “a towering figure on the international scene”—and his faith are worthy of scrutiny.

(CNN) — A video recorded in 2004, in which Tom Cruise discusses his commitment to Scientology, surfaced online this week.

Cruise was also seen with his wife, Katie Holmes, at a film premiere earlier this month.

At the start of the recording, Cruise says that being able to identify as a Scientologist is an honor that must be earned. He adds that he is motivated by the chance to genuinely improve people’s lives and describes himself as completely and unwaveringly committed to that goal.

The footage originally appeared during a 2004 Scientology event at which Cruise was recognized for his humanitarian efforts. Representatives of the Church of Scientology said the recording is available for viewing at all of its churches. It attracted widespread attention this week, however, after what church officials described as an unauthorized, edited copy was uploaded to YouTube.

YouTube later removed the video, although part of the interview could still be watched Thursday on the celebrity website Gawker.com.

Gawker presented the footage under the headline, “The Cruise Indoctrination Video Scientology Tried To Suppress.” The site urged visitors to view it, saying Cruise advocated for Scientology with the same intense, wide-eyed enthusiasm he uses when promoting a film. Gawker characterized Scientology as an unusual religion created in the 20th century.

In the recording, Cruise speaks over a continuously repeated guitar riff. Although he seems to be responding to questions, no interviewer can be seen or heard.

Another section of the footage was provided to CNN by the publisher of a newly released, unauthorized Cruise biography. It shows Cruise receiving Scientology’s Freedom Medal of Valor and exchanging military-style salutes with Church of Scientology chairman David Miscavige as the audience applauds. The publisher said it was not responsible for releasing any other portions of the recording online.

In that version, Cruise also salutes an image of L. Ron Hubbard. The church’s website identifies Hubbard as the founder of what it describes as the only major religion established during the 20th century. Hubbard’s official biography credits him with accomplishments in numerous fields, including sailing, horticulture, writing and humanitarianism.

Cruise places particular emphasis on Hubbard’s humanitarian legacy. He says Scientologists are capable of producing new realities and making circumstances better.

The Church of Scientology’s website promotes the organization’s humanitarian programs, including anti-drug initiatives in locations ranging from Minnesota to Taiwan, as well as teacher-training efforts in India. The site describes Scientology as the pursuit or study of truth.

Cruise echoes that idea in the footage, saying Scientologists are able to perceive reality as it actually is. He also says the faith gives him a sense of calm, explaining that gaining more knowledge through Scientology prevents a person from becoming overwhelmed.

The unauthorized biography was written by Andrew Morton. Both Cruise’s representative and the Church of Scientology challenged the book, arguing that Morton failed to ask them for their views. In a statement, the church said accuracy and truth had not been among Morton’s priorities.

Morton rejected that criticism. He argued that Cruise—whom he described as a major figure internationally—and the actor’s religion deserve examination. Morton also said Cruise has carried out significant work on behalf of Scientology in recent years and claimed the church would be only a fraction of its current prominence without him.

The original report included links to excerpts from the Cruise video, a *Showbiz Tonight* discussion about the footage and an option to e-mail the story to a friend.

CNN’s Brad Lendon, David Mattingly and Don Lemon contributed to the report.

In January 2008, a video recorded several years earlier at a Church of Scientology event appeared online and quickly became a major internet sensation. The footage, made in 2004, featured actor Tom Cruise speaking enthusiastically about Scientology, describing his commitment to its teachings and his belief that Scientologists have a special responsibility to help others. Edited with dramatic music and clips from Cruise’s remarks, the video presented the actor as one of the church’s most prominent and devoted celebrity members.

The footage also showed Cruise receiving the Freedom Medal of Valor, an honor presented by Scientology leader David Miscavige during a church ceremony. Cruise praised Miscavige and spoke in highly emphatic language about applying Scientology principles to social problems, emergencies and everyday life. His intense delivery, combined with the video’s promotional style, attracted widespread attention and prompted extensive discussion in the press, on blogs and across online forums.

The Church of Scientology said the footage had been pirated and taken out of context. It issued copyright complaints in an effort to have copies removed from YouTube and other websites. Those attempts proved controversial and, rather than containing the story, helped generate further interest in the video. News organizations and websites debated whether publishing the footage constituted fair use, while copies and excerpts continued to circulate online.

The episode renewed scrutiny of Cruise’s role as Scientology’s most famous public advocate. It also intensified broader questions about the church’s beliefs, its use of celebrity members and its efforts to control unauthorized material. Critics portrayed the takedown campaign as an attempt to suppress public discussion, while the church maintained that it was protecting copyrighted footage from unauthorized distribution and misleading editing.

Ultimately, the video became an early example of how efforts to remove material from the internet can draw even more attention to it. Cruise’s remarks, the ceremony surrounding his award and Scientology’s response all became part of a larger public debate about the secretive and controversial organization.

counterfactuals.output:
## Cruise Scientology Video Sparks Copyright and Free-Speech Fight

**NEW YORK (CNN-style report)** — A leaked video showing actor Tom Cruise praising the Church of Scientology has ignited an online controversy after it appeared on YouTube and was later posted by the media website Gawker.

The roughly nine-minute clip, reportedly produced for an internal Scientology event, shows Cruise speaking enthusiastically about the responsibilities of church members. In the heavily edited video, the “Mission: Impossible” star says Scientologists are uniquely equipped to help in emergencies and describes the religion as a force for global change.

The video was widely copied and discussed after surfacing online in January 2008. YouTube removed at least one version following a copyright complaint from the Church of Scientology.

Gawker, however, kept the clip on its website despite receiving a legal demand from the church. The site argued that the video was newsworthy and that publishing it was protected under the doctrine of fair use.

The Church of Scientology said the footage had been stolen and edited without authorization, maintaining that it was copyrighted material intended for members. The church also said the excerpts were presented without proper context.

Cruise, one of Scientology’s most prominent members, has previously drawn attention for publicly defending the church and criticizing psychiatry and psychiatric medication.

The dispute quickly expanded beyond celebrity gossip, raising questions about copyright enforcement, online journalism and whether organizations can prevent embarrassing internal material from spreading across the Internet.

It also galvanized critics of Scientology, including the loosely organized online group known as Anonymous, which later staged demonstrations against the church. Scientology representatives have said critics frequently distort its beliefs and target the organization with misinformation.

By the time legal notices were issued, copies of the Cruise video had already circulated across blogs, file-sharing sites and social-media platforms — illustrating the difficulty of containing controversial material once it reaches the Web.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the leaked Tom Cruise Scientology indoctrination video, including the church’s response, Andrew Morton’s biography, and Cruise’s statements about his faith.
counterfactuals.output:
### Leaked Scientology video

The roughly nine-minute video, leaked online in January 2008, was excerpted from an internal Church of Scientology production recorded several years earlier. Against music from *Mission: Impossible*, Tom Cruise speaks intensely about the obligations of Scientologists and uses church terminology such as “KSW” (“Keeping Scientology Working”) and “SPs” (“suppressive persons”).

Cruise argues that Scientologists possess unique knowledge and therefore have a special responsibility to intervene in society. Among his most discussed remarks were that, when encountering an accident, a Scientologist is “the only one that can really help,” and that Scientologists are authorities on rehabilitation and the mind. He also says membership demands complete commitment: “You’re either on board or you’re not,” and calls it a privilege to be a Scientologist. The video’s abrupt edits, jargon, laughter, and highly emphatic delivery made it appear especially strange to viewers outside the church.

### Church of Scientology’s response

The church said the footage was intended for a private Scientology audience and had been selectively edited and presented without the context needed to understand its terminology. It pursued copyright complaints and sent legal demands to websites hosting it, including Gawker, arguing that distribution was unauthorized. Critics characterized those efforts as censorship; widespread reposting ultimately made the video more prominent.

The church also defended Cruise as a committed humanitarian and said the excerpt distorted a longer presentation concerning Scientology’s social programs, including drug rehabilitation, literacy, and disaster relief.

### Andrew Morton’s biography

The leak coincided with publication of Andrew Morton’s *Tom Cruise: An Unauthorized Biography*. Morton portrayed Cruise as deeply embedded in Scientology and exceptionally close to church leader David Miscavige. The book also made controversial claims about the church’s influence over Cruise’s personal relationships, his family, and his public conduct, and suggested that Cruise held unusually high status within the organization.

Cruise’s representatives and the Church of Scientology rejected the book as inaccurate, defamatory, and religiously prejudiced. The church issued detailed rebuttals, while Morton maintained that his account was based on extensive interviews and research. Many of the book’s most sensational assertions depended on unnamed sources and remain disputed rather than established facts.

### Cruise’s public statements about his faith

Cruise has repeatedly credited Scientology with helping him overcome childhood dyslexia, giving him practical tools for communication and study, and improving his life. He has described himself as a committed Scientologist and has promoted church-affiliated humanitarian and educational programs.

His advocacy became particularly controversial in 2005, when he criticized psychiatry and psychiatric medication, condemned Brooke Shields’s use of medication for postpartum depression, and argued with Matt Lauer on NBC’s *Today* about antidepressants. He later apologized personally to Shields, though he did not renounce Scientology’s broader opposition to psychiatry.

Taken together, the leaked video, Morton’s biography, and Cruise’s own interviews depict a celebrity whose faith is central to his identity—but they differ sharply over whether that commitment represents personal conviction and humanitarian activism, as Cruise and the church contend, or extraordinary institutional influence, as Morton and other critics argue.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
